title: "Architecture"
lang: en-US
toc: true
---

This page describes how `SimilaritySearchEngine.jl` is put together: its module map, the
engine type hierarchy that replaces name/enum-based dispatch with real Julia types, the
staging-vs-indexing split that lets a project decouple insertion from the expensive
graph-connection/encoding step (dense *and* full-text alike), the concurrency model that
lets searches run in parallel while staying safe from concurrent inserts, and the
RocksDB-column-families-plus-one-mmap-file layout that makes persistence incremental
instead of a single ever-growing blob.

## Module map

The package is five source files, four of them real submodules (`Schema`, `Project`,
`IndexEngine`, `Persistence`) plus `embedded.jl`, which defines `EmbeddedEngine` and the
top-level functions (`create_project`, `append_items!`, `search`, ...) directly in the
`SimilaritySearchEngine` module itself — the friendly surface a script actually calls.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Schema["Schema<br/><small>MetadataRecord (_id, doc_id,<br/>keywords, refs), meta split</small>"]
    Project["Project<br/><small>ProjectManager, metadata CRUD</small>"]
    IndexEngine["IndexEngine<br/><small>AbstractSearchEngine hierarchy</small>"]
    Persistence["Persistence<br/><small>EngineStore, AdjacencyStore, ...</small>"]
    Embedded["embedded.jl<br/><small>EmbeddedEngine + top-level API</small>"]
    Caller(["Julia script, or<br/>SimilaritySearchServer"])

    Schema --> Project
    Schema --> Embedded
    Project --> Embedded
    IndexEngine --> Embedded
    Persistence --> Embedded
    Embedded --> Caller
```

`IndexEngine` and `Persistence` are deliberately independent of `Project`/`Schema` and of
each other: `IndexEngine` knows nothing about RocksDB (its persistence hook is a plain
`(index, sp, ep) -> nothing` callback), and `Persistence` knows nothing about metadata
schemas or search engines (it stores plain Julia values under string keys). `embedded.jl`
is the one place that wires all four together — every other module could, in principle,
be reused on its own.

`Schema`/`Project` have no per-project typed-field schema to declare anymore: every
project has exactly the same fixed-shape `Schema.MetadataRecord` (`_id`, `doc_id`,
`keywords`, `refs`) plus a free-form `meta` JSON blob for everything else appended with an
item — `_id` is the internal, sequential, always-present handle (the same id space the
engine's own vector/text store uses); `doc_id` is the caller's own external id, if any;
`keywords`/`refs` are the only two fields with a secondary index (`Project`'s fixed
`idx_keywords`/`idx_refs` column families), everything else lives in `meta`, looked up
straight from `Project`, never indexed.

## Engine type hierarchy

A project is two decisions, and the hierarchy keeps them apart: an **engine** says what the
project holds, and a **backend** says which index holds it.

```{julia}
#| eval: false
create_project(w, ds)                                              # dense vectors, SearchGraph
create_project(w, ds; engine=DenseEngine, backend=ExhaustiveSearch)
create_project(w, ds; engine=SparseEngine, dimension=50_000)
create_project(w, ds; engine=FullTextEngine, backend=BM25InvertedFile,
                      textmodel=DefaultProfile(:es))
```

Three engines, because there are three kinds of thing a caller can hand over — a dense vector,
a sparse vector, a string — and each needs a different amount of machinery to accept it. Four
backends, because there are four ways to hold an index and they carry different state. There is
still no enum tag anywhere: the concrete Julia type is what `add_item!`, `search_live` and every
other generic function dispatch on, and `DenseEngine{B}` dispatches on its backend too.

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    class AbstractSearchEngine {
        <<abstract>>
    }
    class DenseEngine~B~ {
        backend: B
        search_ctx_pool: ContextPool
        deleted_ids: Set~UInt32~
        lock: ReadWriteLock
    }
    class SparseEngine {
        backend: SparseBackend
        search_ctx_pool: ContextPool
        deleted_ids: Set~UInt32~
        lock: ReadWriteLock
    }
    class FullTextEngine {
        backend: TextBackend
        profile: Union~Nothing, TextProfile~
        fitspec: Union~Nothing, DeferredFit~
        staged: Vector~String~
        search_ctx_pool: ContextPool
        deleted_ids: Set~UInt32~
        lock: ReadWriteLock
    }
    class GraphBackend {
        index: SearchGraph
        ctx: SearchGraphContext
        minrecall: Union~Nothing, Float32~
        opt_beamsearch: OptBeamSearch
    }
    class ExactBackend~IndexType~ {
        index: IndexType
        ctx: GenericContext
    }
    class SparseBackend {
        index: InvertedFile
        ctx: InvertedFileContext
        distance: PreMetric
        dimension: Int
    }
    class TextBackend {
        index: Union~Nothing, AbstractInvertedFile~
        ctx: InvertedFileContext
        kind: Type
        distance: Union~Nothing, PreMetric~
    }
    AbstractSearchEngine <|-- DenseEngine
    AbstractSearchEngine <|-- SparseEngine
    AbstractSearchEngine <|-- FullTextEngine
    DenseEngine *-- GraphBackend
    DenseEngine *-- ExactBackend
    SparseEngine *-- SparseBackend
    FullTextEngine *-- TextBackend
```

A few design choices worth calling out:

- **The split exists because of `SparseEngine`.** Before it, the hierarchy was one struct per
  index kind — a `SearchGraphEngine`, a `GenericEngine{IndexType}`, a `BM25Engine`, an
  `InvertedFileEngine` — which sorted projects by the thing a caller is least likely to know and
  most likely to change. It also left a hole: an `InvertedFile` and its distance were reachable
  only *through* a text engine, so a caller who already held sparse vectors had to pretend to
  have text — fit a profile it did not want, stage strings it did not have. `SparseEngine` is
  that missing layer, and separating the two decisions is what made it expressible.
- **`payload_kind(engine)`** returns `:dense`, `:sparse` or `:text`, and is what guards ask
  instead of the `is_text_index` predicate they used to. With two kinds, "not text" meant
  "dense"; with three that reading is simply false.
- **`BACKENDS`** is the table of legal pairings, read three ways — to default a backend, to
  check one, and to name the alternatives in the error when a check fails. `InvertedFile`
  appears under both `SparseEngine` and `FullTextEngine` on purpose: the same library index
  serves sparse vectors a caller encoded and text this package encodes, and `engine` is what
  says which. Three methods instead of one table would drift; the table cannot.
- **BM25 is not one of `SparseEngine`'s distances**, which is the one asymmetry worth
  explaining. `BM25InvertedFile` holds a `Vocabulary` and scores from `getndocs`/`avgdoclen`:
  BM25 is a scoring rule over a corpus, not a metric over sparse vectors. So it stays with
  `FullTextEngine`, which has the corpus statistics, and `SparseEngine` takes the distances that
  read a vector — cosine over the weights, or one of `Dist.Sets.*` over the nonzero positions.
- `minrecall`/`opt_beamsearch` live on `GraphBackend` and nowhere else — only a `SearchGraph`
  autotunes a `BeamSearch` toward a target recall. On the engine they would be two fields every
  exact and every inverted-file project could only ever leave empty.
- `SparseBackend` records the `dimension` it was created with, and `create_project` requires it
  for a sparse project. An `InvertedFile` is a fixed array of posting lists: the dimension is
  structural, not descriptive, so it has to be known before the first item and every item
  appended has to agree with it.
- `FullTextEngine` carries its whole text model in one field,
  `profile::Union{Nothing, TextProfile}` — vocabulary and weights (`profile.model`) plus the
  corpus-produced artifacts (stopword set, lemma map, query-expansion network) and the
  lineage saying how it was produced. That replaced a `voc`/`model` pair carried before
  `TextSearch` 1.1 published `TextProfile`, and the reason to prefer it is structural: an
  artifact has exactly one home, and the `TextConfig` the tokenizer runs is *derived* from the
  profile, so an index cannot end up tokenizing documents through a different lemma map than
  the one it saves.
- A text project is created from an `AbstractTextModelSpec`: three answers to "where does the
  vocabulary come from", not variations on one setting. `BaseProfile(profile)` trains it at
  creation. `DefaultProfile(:es)` and `FitFromCorpus(textconfig; …)` leave it untrained and
  store the recipe in `fitspec`, for the first `index!` call to carry out — the first by loading
  the published profile for that language and refitting it against the staged corpus, the second
  by delegating a fit of it to `TextSearch.fit_profile`. `index === nothing` exactly while
  `profile === nothing`. There is no separate training entry point:
  `add_item!`/`append_items!` always just stage raw text into `staged` (never an error,
  trained or not — see "Staging vs. indexing" below).
- **Fitting is the library's job, not this package's.** `train_profile` is a dispatcher over
  the two deferred specs and nothing more: one calls `TextSearch.fit_profile`, the other
  `TextSearch.load_profile` + `TextSearch.refit_profile`. This package used to fit a vocabulary
  and weights itself, and every line of that was a second implementation of something the
  library does. What delegation costs is that a fit is now the *full* pipeline — LSI, expansion
  network, lemma clustering — with no cheap variant, which is why `FitFromCorpus` caps its
  sample at `max_documents` and why the recommended path avoids fitting altogether.
- `create_project` **requires** the spec for a text project and refuses `nothing`, and the other
  two kinds refuse a spec rather than ignoring one. Both directions are deliberate. The
  fit-from-corpus form freezes the vocabulary at the first `index!` call, so every term a later
  batch introduces is dropped from then on — nothing about the project's behaviour afterwards
  distinguishes "I chose this" from "I never said", which is exactly why it cannot be a default.
  In the other direction, a text model handed to an index of vectors has no reading under which
  it does anything, so swallowing it is how a project ends up not being the kind its author
  thought it was. Each spec is a type carrying its *own* options, so an option that only
  means something on one path cannot be handed to the other — the same reason this hierarchy
  discriminates on concrete types instead of an enum tag.
- **Query-side orthographic bridging is the library's too.** This engine used to derive and
  cache a variant map itself (`musica` → `música`) in a `variants` field. `TextSearch` 1.1 builds
  that map inside the index's own `QueryPipeline`, so the field is gone and a `QueryPolicy`
  passed to `ftsearch` modifies how the existing map is *applied* rather than rebuilding it. One
  map, in the index that owns it.
- Every engine shares three fields regardless of what else it carries: `deleted_ids::Set{UInt32}`
  (logically deleted document ids — `UInt32` uniformly, matching the id type search
  results actually come back as), `lock::ReadWriteLock`, and `search_ctx_pool::ContextPool`
  (see below).

## Staging vs. indexing: a graph and a text project have the split, the rest index on insertion

`append_items!`/`add_item!` only ever *stages* an item for a graph-backed dense project and for
a text one; `search_live`/`ftsearch`/`allknn`/`fft`/`closestpairs`/`bichromatic_kclosestpairs`
only ever see items an explicit `index!` call has actually processed, not merely staged.

The other two backends have no split to speak of. An exact index (`ExhaustiveSearch`/
`ParallelExhaustiveSearch`) always evaluates directly against `db`, and an `InvertedFile` builds
its posting lists on insertion, so for both of them `append_items!` makes an item searchable
immediately. `index!` is still defined for them, as a no-op: the same four lines —
`create_project`, `append_items!`, `index!`, `search` — should mean the same thing for every kind
of project, and a caller should not have to know which backends need the third one. The cost is a
call that does nothing, which is the cheaper mistake; the alternative made switching a project
from a graph to a brute-force scan a change to every script that fed it.

`SimilaritySearch.jl`'s own `SearchGraph` separates *staging* raw vectors into its
database from the (expensive) graph-connection work, and this package extends that same
split to the text backends, which have no such native support of their own to lean on:

- graph-backed dense: `insert_dense!(index::SearchGraph, ctx, item) = push_item!(index.db, item)`
  only ever appends `item` to `index.db` — cheap, and durable the instant it happens (see
  Persistence below), but `index.adj` (the graph itself) is untouched.
  `IndexEngine.index!(engine::DenseEngine{GraphBackend})` is the explicit, idempotent step that
  actually builds graph connections for whatever has been staged since the last call (or
  since creation) — it delegates to `SimilaritySearch.index!(engine.index, engine.ctx)`,
  which itself only ever processes the backlog (`length(engine.index)+1:length(database(engine.index))`),
  so calling it repeatedly, or with nothing new staged, is a cheap no-op.
- text: `add_item!` just pushes raw text onto `engine.staged`
  — the text-engine counterpart of `index.db`, since `TextSearch.jl`'s inverted-file types
  have no raw-item staging area of their own to reuse. `IndexEngine.index!(engine)` (no
  corpus argument) catches up the exact same backlog range
  (`(engine.index === nothing ? 0 : length(engine.index))+1:length(engine.staged)`),
  encoding each staged text (`bagofwords` for BM25; for the weighted engine, handing the
  text straight to `TextInvertedFile`, whose own `push_item!` vectorizes through the
  profile's model) and `push_item!`ing it into the real index — with one extra twist on its
  *first* call for a project created without a profile: since neither index kind can even be
  constructed without a `Vocabulary`, that call runs the engine's `fitspec` over what is staged
  so far and builds the real index against the resulting `TextProfile`, before running the same
  backlog loop. Every later call is a plain catch-up, identical in shape to the graph's.

  A project created from a `BaseProfile` skips that entirely, and the difference is not only
  when the work happens: a vocabulary fitted from a sample of the first batch is frozen there,
  so every term appended later that it never saw is out-of-vocabulary and silently dropped.
  Starting from a profile fitted over the language — `DefaultProfile(:es)`, or a `BaseProfile`
  of one you hold — is what makes an incrementally-grown text project behave.

This decouples *when* an item becomes durable (immediately, on `append_items!`) from
*when* it becomes searchable (only after an explicit `index!`), so a caller controls when
the expensive graph-connection/encoding cost is paid — once per big batch, on a schedule,
or right before the next round of queries — instead of paying it synchronously on every
single insert the way an exact or an inverted-file backend does.

## Concurrency model

None of the underlying index kinds tolerates a search running concurrently with an
insertion into the *same* index — a search reading `index.adj`/`index.db` while
`add_item!` resizes/appends to those same arrays is exactly the kind of concurrent
read-during-mutation none of them are built for. But all of them *do* safely support running
multiple searches concurrently against the same index, since that is exactly what their
own `searchbatch`/`allknn` parallel paths already rely on internally.

### `ReadWriteLock`

Each engine's `lock` is a custom reader/writer lock (built from a `Threads.Condition` plus
a reader count), not a plain `ReentrantLock`: `search_live`/`current_beamsearch` take it as
a *read* lock (any number of readers concurrently), while `add_item!`/`index!`/
`mark_deleted!`/`calibrate!` take it as a *write* lock (exclusive of every reader and every
other writer).

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant S1 as search_live (thread 1)
    participant S2 as search_live (thread 2)
    participant W as add_item! (thread 3)
    participant L as engine.lock

    S1->>L: read_lock (readers 0 to 1)
    S2->>L: read_lock (readers 1 to 2)
    Note over S1,S2: both searches run concurrently
    W->>L: write_lock (blocks: readers > 0)
    S1->>L: release (readers 2 to 1)
    S2->>L: release (readers 1 to 0)
    L->>W: write lock granted
    Note over W: insert_dense! / push_item! using engine.ctx
    W->>L: release
```

A read-to-write "upgrade" on the same logical operation would deadlock (the write lock
waits for the reader count to hit zero, including the reader this same call is itself
holding) — so a graph backend's `minrecall`-driven auto-`calibrate!` inside
`search_live` is always resolved *before* the read lock is acquired, never nested inside
it.

### `ContextPool`

Guarding the index data isn't enough by itself: `SearchGraphContext`/`GenericContext`/
`InvertedFileContext` are all *mutable, reused* scratch spaces (beam buffers,
visited-vertices state, per-batch cost counters, ...), and two concurrent searches sharing
the same context object corrupt each other's scratch state — confirmed directly by a
segfault inside `SearchGraph`'s own beam search when two threads raced on a shared
context.

`ContextPool` avoids both bad alternatives — sharing one context (unsafe) and allocating a
fresh one on every single call (wasteful, since these contexts are non-trivial to
allocate) — by handing each concurrent `search_live` call its own checked-out context,
returned to the pool when done:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["search_live call"] --> B{"pool.available<br/>non-empty?"}
    B -- yes --> C["pop! an idle context"]
    B -- no --> D["deepcopy(pool.template)"]
    C --> E["run the search with this context"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["checkin!: push! back onto pool.available"]
```

The pool grows lazily to (and then stays at) however many concurrent searches an engine
has actually seen at once — never pre-allocated speculatively, never shrunk either. `ctx`
itself (the engine's own field) is never touched by `search_live`; it stays reserved for
insertion, which already runs under an exclusive `write_lock`, so sharing it there is
safe.

## Persistence: one storage unit per concern

Earlier iterations of this design re-serialized the *entire* engine state — including the
whole index — on every mutation. The current design instead gives each kind of state its
own RocksDB column family (or, for a `SearchGraph`'s raw vectors, its own file outside
RocksDB entirely — see below), so a mutation only ever rewrites the storage it actually
touched.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    subgraph db["one RocksDB directory per project"]
        records[("records<br/><small>_id → MetadataRecord (fixed shape)</small>")]
        meta[("meta<br/><small>_id → free-form meta (JSON)</small>")]
        oplog[("op_log")]
        idxkw[("idx_keywords<br/><small>keyword → _ids</small>")]
        idxrefs[("idx_refs<br/><small>referenced doc_id → _ids</small>")]
        engine[("engine <small>(ENGINE_CF)</small><br/><small>one key per engine struct field</small>")]
        adj[("searchgraph_adj <small>(ADJACENCY_CF)</small><br/><small>object_id → direct neighbors</small>")]
        stagedtext[("staged_text <small>(STAGED_TEXT_CF)</small><br/><small>append-only raw, not-yet-encoded text blocks</small>")]
        sparsedb[("sparse_db <small>(INVFILE_DB_CF)</small><br/><small>append-only encoded object blocks</small>")]
    end
    mmapfile[["dense_vectors.mmapdb<br/><small>-- not RocksDB --<br/>one row per staged vector</small>"]]

    ProjectManager -- "put_metadata! / get_metadata" --> records
    ProjectManager -- "get_meta / get_raw_meta" --> meta
    ProjectManager -- "secondary lookups" --> idxkw
    ProjectManager -- "secondary lookups" --> idxrefs
    EngineStore -- "save_field! / load_field" --> engine
    AdjacencyStore -- "save_neighbors! / load_neighbors" --> adj
    StagedTextStore -- "append_staged_texts! / load_staged_text_blocks" --> stagedtext
    InvertedFileObjectStore -- "append_objects! / load_object_blocks" --> sparsedb
    append_items_dense["append_items!<br/>(SearchGraph)"] --> mmapfile
    append_items_text["append_items!<br/>(BM25InvertedFile/InvertedFile)"] --> stagedtext
```

Every RocksDB column family above lives in the *same* directory/connection as the
project's metadata store (`Project.ProjectManager.db`) — `Project.open_project`'s
`extra_cf_names` keyword is how `IndexEngine`'s persistence layer gets its own column
families listed alongside `Project`'s, since every column family that exists on disk must
be named at `opendb` time on *every* open, not only the first. `dense_vectors.mmapdb` is
the one exception: a plain file, alongside (not inside) the RocksDB directory -- raw text
has no fixed-size-record shape to exploit that way, so `staged_text` stays a RocksDB
column family, structured exactly like `sparse_db` (append-only, blocks keyed by starting
position) but holding *raw, un-encoded* text instead of already-encoded objects.

### `EngineStore`: per-field keys, not one blob

`EngineStore` is a `field_name::Symbol => value` map, one RocksDB key per struct field.
`save_field!`/`load_field` touch exactly one key; `save_fields!` is only used for rare,
one-shot multi-field transitions (right after `create_engine`, or the moment a text
engine's vocabulary is first trained). A soft delete only ever rewrites `:deleted_ids`; a
`calibrate!` call only ever rewrites `:opt_beamsearch`.

### Dense vectors: a memory-mapped file, not a RocksDB column family

A graph-backed project's raw vectors are fixed-dimension `Float32` data — exactly what
`SimilaritySearch.MMapMatrixDatabase` is for, and its own append-only counter/growth/fsync
discipline already gives durable, in-order, crash-safe storage with no need for
RocksDB's batch-keying scheme, at a much cheaper per-vector read than a RocksDB point
lookup (confirmed empirically against `VectorDatabase`/`BlockMatrixDatabase` in
`SimilaritySearch.jl`'s own test suite). `append_items!` writes staged vectors directly
into this file, at stage time — not through `CallbackLog` at all, unlike everything else
in this section — since a vector is durable-worthy the moment it's staged, long before any
graph-linking work happens. The file (`dense_vectors.mmapdb`) is created lazily, on the
first dense append, since its dimension isn't known before then.

Batch size matters a lot here: `MMapMatrixDatabase` `fsync`s once per `append_items!`
call, never per individual vector, so the number of calls a caller makes (not the total
vector count) drives wall-clock time — confirmed empirically, 200,000 128-dim vectors as
one 200,000-item call took ~0.10s; the same total split into calls of 10 items took
~2.1s; one call per single item measured roughly 1000x slower than the all-at-once case.
Prefer fewer, larger `append_items!` calls over many small ones.

### Incremental adjacency/posting-list persistence: different shapes, by necessity

The graph/posting-list structure itself is the other expensive, ever-growing part, so it
is never saved as a single value either. Its incremental format is driven by
`SimilaritySearch.CallbackLog`, an *observer* that fires a `flush(index, sp, ep)` callback
on every `:add!` event a mutating call reports — `SimilaritySearch.jl` standardizes every
index kind's structural events onto this one name, regardless of which entry point
triggered it, and the observation channel carries nothing else, so `CallbackLog` never has
to branch on the event itself. What *does* differ by index kind is the *shape* of what gets
saved, and *when* this callback fires relative to `append_items!`.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller as index!(handle)
    participant Idx as SearchGraph
    participant CB as CallbackLog
    participant ES as EngineStore
    participant AS as AdjacencyStore

    Note over Caller,Idx: append_items! already staged vectors into<br/>dense_vectors.mmapdb -- no CallbackLog involved
    Caller->>Idx: SimilaritySearch.index!(engine.index, ctx)
    Idx->>Idx: build graph connections for the staged backlog (range sp:ep)
    Idx->>CB: LOG(:add!, index, ctx, sp, ep)
    Note right of Idx: fires BEFORE connect_reverse_links!<br/>index.adj[sp:ep] holds only direct links
    CB->>AS: save_neighbors!(i, direct_neighbors(i)) for i in sp:ep
    CB->>ES: save_field!(:graph_len, ep)
    Idx->>Idx: connect_reverse_links! (in memory only)
```

For a `SearchGraph`, `LOG` fires *before* `connect_reverse_links!` runs for that range —
so what's captured at that instant is exactly the direct-links-only slice. This is by
design, not a bug to route around: `connect_reverse_links!` isn't idempotent (re-running
it on an already-complete graph would duplicate reverse edges), so the on-disk format
never saves reverse links at all. `:graph_len` (how far graph-indexing actually got,
which can lag behind how many vectors are staged in `dense_vectors.mmapdb` if the process
closed between an `append_items!` and its follow-up `index!`) lets reloading resume
exactly where indexing left off, over the same, already-fully-restored `.db`.

The inverted-file backends — `BM25InvertedFile` and `TextInvertedFile` for a text project,
`InvertedFile` for a sparse one — have no direct/reverse-link hazard: their own `LOG` only
fires after a `push_item!` call's mutation is fully done, so `InvertedFileObjectStore`
simply appends the raw encoded objects just inserted (`invertedfile_objects`) as a new
block. For a **text** project that `LOG` fires from *inside* an `index!` call's backlog loop
(see "Staging vs. indexing" above) rather than from `append_items!` directly — `append_items!`
only ever writes to `StagedTextStore`, the raw-text counterpart of `dense_vectors.mmapdb`, and
`sparse_db`'s already-encoded blocks only grow once an `index!` call actually catches the
backlog up. For a **sparse** project there is no such indirection and no `StagedTextStore` at
all: the caller handed over the encoded vector itself, so the insertion *is* the encoding and
the block is written on `append_items!`.
Reloading `index` itself still rebuilds the whole thing by replaying every saved *encoded*
object back through the library's own `push_item!` — a rebuild-by-reinsertion design, not
a real on-disk posting-list format — while `staged` (every raw text ever staged, whether
or not it's been encoded yet) is restored separately, straight from `StagedTextStore`, and
handed to `restore_engine` alongside `object_blocks`. This is a deliberate scaling limit,
not an oversight: it's fine up to a few million documents, since the whole corpus and the
whole rebuilt index have to fit in memory and reloading costs the full original indexing
time again. It is *not* a design for billion-document corpora, which need genuinely
disk-backed, paged-on-demand posting lists.

An exact backend (`ExhaustiveSearch`/`ParallelExhaustiveSearch`) has no incremental format
of its own — its `on_change` just flags `pending_flush[]`, and `embedded.jl` saves the
*whole* index as a single `:index` value right after the triggering `add_item!` call
returns. This is acceptable for these exact, in-memory-only index kinds, which have no
adjacency or posting-list structure to split apart in the first place, and index
synchronously on every `add_item!`.

### Reopening a project

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller as open_project
    participant MM as dense_vectors.mmapdb
    participant ES as EngineStore
    participant AS as AdjacencyStore
    participant IE as IndexEngine

    Caller->>ES: load_field(:kind)
    Caller->>MM: open_dense_vectors(dir) → vector_blocks (one block, every staged vector)
    Caller->>AS: load_neighbors(i) for i in 1:graph_len
    Caller->>ES: load_field(:graph_len, 0)
    Caller->>IE: build_searchgraph(distance, vector_blocks, load_neighbors, graph_len)
    IE->>IE: replay every staged vector into index.db (in full)
    IE->>IE: add! each of the first graph_len objects' saved direct neighbors
    IE->>IE: connect_reverse_links! once, over 1:graph_len
    IE-->>Caller: reconstructed SearchGraph -- index.len[] = graph_len
    Caller->>IE: restore_engine(state, on_change) → DenseEngine{GraphBackend}
```

`graph_len` can be `<= length(index.db)`: every staged vector is always fully restored
into `.db` (that's durable from the moment it was staged), but only the first `graph_len`
of them were ever graph-indexed before the project last closed — if it closed between an
`append_items!` and its follow-up `index!` call, the gap is restored as staged-but-not-yet-
searchable, waiting on a future `index!(handle)` call to catch it up, exactly as it was
before closing.

`restore_engine` dispatches on `Val(state.kind)` — `:dense`, `:sparse` or `:text` — and each
branch then reads `state.backend` to pick the index within that kind. Both are **symbols, not
Julia types**, and that is what makes a saved project survive this file being rewritten: the
previous shape persisted the type `BM25Engine` into the project's own store, so renaming the
types (which this restructuring did to every one of them) made every existing project
unreadable by construction. A symbol cuts that tie, and an unrecognised one maps to an error
naming the ones the reader does know instead of a `MethodError` about a type it has never
heard of.

`IndexEngine.extra_state_fields` only covers the exact backends, and covers them with `()` —
their whole index is a single `:index` field, so there is nothing extra to list. No other
backend has such a field at all: each needs its own combination of `EngineStore` reads
(`:minrecall`/`:opt_beamsearch` for a graph; `:distance`/`:dimension` for a sparse project;
`:profile`/`:fitspec`/`:distance` for a text one) *plus* its own dedicated block-store reads
(`vector_blocks`/`load_neighbors`/`graph_len` for a graph; `object_blocks`/`staged` for the
inverted-file kinds), assembled by hand in `open_project` rather than driven by a generic
per-kind field list.

## Logging: informative output and persistence are independent

Every engine's context carries **two** logging slots, and that split is what makes the
independence structural instead of a convention to remember. This engine used to hand-roll
it — one slot holding three backends of two different kinds, with a comment explaining
which of them could affect persistence — until `SimilaritySearch.jl` grew the distinction
itself.

- **`ctx.reporters`** — where progress goes to be *read*. Always at least one
  `InformativeLog` printing a throttled status line to `stderr`; a `log_io` adds a second
  one writing the same line to any caller-given `IO` (an open file handle, or
  `stdout`/`stderr`). Purely informative, and it cannot be anything else: a reporter is
  only ever handed a message.
- **`ctx.observers`** — what *reacts* to a structural change. A `CallbackLog` here forwards
  every `:add!` report, untouched by any throttling, to whatever `on_change` closure
  `embedded.jl` installed. This is the actual persistence trigger.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Mutation["push_item! / append_items!"] --> INFORM["INFORM<br/>(ctx.reporters)"]
    Mutation --> OBSERVE["OBSERVE :add!<br/>(ctx.observers)"]
    INFORM --> Stderr["InformativeLog<br/>→ stderr, throttled"]
    INFORM --> FileIO["InformativeLog(log_io)<br/>→ any IO, throttled<br/>(optional)"]
    OBSERVE --> CallbackLog["CallbackLog<br/>→ on_change(index, sp, ep)<br/>(persistence trigger)"]
```

The two channels cannot interfere. Silencing the console is `reporters=[]`, and persistence
continues untouched; conversely no observer can be lost by turning output down, because
turning output down does not reach that slot.

## Soft deletes

`mark_deleted!` adds a document's id to `deleted_ids` and nothing else — the underlying
index is never touched, so no rebuild or backfill is needed. `search_live` reports a
`deleted` flag per candidate instead of silently dropping deleted candidates and
backfilling with the next-best live one: compensating for deletions by overfetching would
have to grow with the total number of deletions, and it would hide from the caller which
ids were even considered. A caller that wants `k` *live* results after filtering is
expected to page for more (e.g. via a cursor over successive top-`k'` windows) at a layer
above this one — `SimilaritySearchServer`, not this package.

## Whole-dataset operations

`allknn`, `fft`, `closestpairs`, and `bichromatic_kclosestpairs` all run synchronously,
in-process, directly against a dense project's index — no job queue, unlike the HTTP
API's `POST /api/v1/jobs/allknn`. Each does real work proportional to the *whole* dataset
(or two datasets, for the bichromatic case): `allknn` is every item's own top-`k`
neighbors at once; `fft` (Farthest-First-Traversal) picks `k` well-separated items for
diverse sampling; `closestpairs` finds the `k` globally closest pairs within one project
(near-duplicate/echo detection); `bichromatic_kclosestpairs` finds the `k` closest pairs
between a project's own index and a second, unindexed collection of vectors. All four
require a graph-backed dense project that's had `index!` run at least once — none
apply to a text project.

## Where this leaves `SimilaritySearchServer`

This package covers project lifecycle, core CRUD, calibration, and the whole-dataset
operations above. Pagination policy over soft-deleted results, HTTP/CLI surfaces, job
queues, and telemetry all live one layer up, in the sibling `SimilaritySearchServer`
package, which depends on this one and is kept in sync with it as this package's design
settles.
